steps.explanationAfterStep: The new N–N bond. Only free aniline can do this, which is why the acid is not in huge excess: most of the amine is present as the anilinium ion, which has no lone pair.
Losing a proton gives a neutral N-nitrosamine. For a secondary amine the reaction stops here; a primary amine still has a hydrogen on nitrogen and goes on.
The positive charge is shared with the aniline nitrogen through the N–N bond (draw the other resonance form).
The hydrogen has moved from nitrogen to oxygen in two proton transfers, and N=N has replaced N=O: a tautomer, like an enol from a ketone.
Protonating the OH makes water the leaving group, as in making NO⁺.

The diazonium ion, Ar–N⁺≡N, linear like an alkyne. It is kept cold (0–5 °C): an aryl diazonium ion is stabilised by the ring, but on warming it loses nitrogen gas. Breaking only the N–O bond is also accepted: it is another drawing of the same ion.

title: Diazotisation of aniline
subtitle: Aniline and NO⁺ give the benzenediazonium ion
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 23

reactants.caption: aniline + nitrosonium ion + water
hintTiers: The amine nitrogen is the nucleophile. Which atom of NO⁺ is electrophilic, and where can the electrons of the triple bond go?
The amine lone pair forms a new N–N bond to the nitrogen of NO⁺, and one π bond of N≡O moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Amine N lone pair → new N–N bond to the nitrogen of NO⁺; one N≡O π bond → a lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The formal positive charge is drawn on oxygen, but oxygen keeps its electrons tightly. Nitrogen is the electrophilic end of NO⁺ (think of the N⁺=O drawing).
Water adding to NO⁺ only makes nitrous acid again. The amine is the better nucleophile.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right atoms. Nitrogen of NO⁺ now has five bonds: move one N≡O π pair onto oxygen.

n-nitrosamine.caption: N-nitrosoaniline + hydronium ion
hintTiers: The proton on the aniline nitrogen has to end up on oxygen. In acid, add a proton first. Which atom has a lone pair that gives a cation shared with the other nitrogen?
The N=O oxygen uses a lone pair to take the drawn proton from H₃O⁺, and that O–H pair stays on water's oxygen. Two arrows.
N=O oxygen lone pair → new bond to the drawn H of H₃O⁺; that O–H bond → a lone pair on water's oxygen.
n-nitrosamine.learnerPrompt: Proton shuffle, part 1: H₃O⁺ protonates the N-nitroso compound.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Protonating the aniline nitrogen leads back to the N-nitrosoanilinium ion. Protonate the oxygen: the hydrogen has to end up there.
That nitrogen's lone pair is not where the proton ends up. Protonate the oxygen.

diazohydroxide.caption: a diazohydroxide (Ph–N=N–OH) + hydronium ion
hintTiers: As in making NO⁺, an OH group becomes a leaving group once it is protonated.
The OH oxygen takes the drawn proton from H₃O⁺, and that O–H pair stays on water's oxygen. Two arrows.
OH oxygen lone pair → new bond to the drawn H of H₃O⁺; that O–H bond → a lone pair on water's oxygen.
diazohydroxide.learnerPrompt: Protonate the OH group so that it can leave.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Protonating a nitrogen creates no leaving group. Protonate the OH: it leaves as water.

n-nitrosoanilinium.caption: N-nitrosoanilinium ion + water
hintTiers: The new N–N bond leaves the aniline nitrogen positive with two hydrogens. Which molecule is the base?
The water lone pair takes one of the drawn hydrogens on the positive nitrogen, and the N–H pair stays on nitrogen. Two arrows.
Water O lone pair → new bond to a drawn H on the positive nitrogen; that N–H bond → a lone pair on that nitrogen.
n-nitrosoanilinium.learnerPrompt: Water takes a proton from the positive nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the new N–N bond only returns to aniline and NO⁺. Lose a proton instead.

protonated-nitrosamine.caption: O-protonated N-nitrosoaniline + water
hintTiers: Losing the N–H proton should leave a lone pair that can form a π bond. Where does the N=O π pair go?
Water takes the drawn hydrogen on the aniline nitrogen; that N–H pair forms an N=N π bond, and the N=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Three arrows.
Water O lone pair → new bond to the drawn H on the aniline nitrogen; that N–H bond → an N=N π bond; the N=O π bond → a lone pair on oxygen.
protonated-nitrosamine.learnerPrompt: Proton shuffle, part 2: water removes the N–H proton and an N=N bond forms.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the O–H proton back just undoes the last step. Remove the proton on the aniline nitrogen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the N=N bond forms. Now the middle nitrogen has too many bonds: move the N=O π pair onto oxygen.

protonated-diazohydroxide.caption: protonated diazohydroxide + water
hintTiers: The N–OH₂⁺ bond can break. Which lone pair can form a third bond between the nitrogens?
The lone pair of the nitrogen attached to the ring forms a second π bond to the other nitrogen, and the N–O bond breaks onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Lone pair of the ring nitrogen → another N–N π bond; the N–O bond → a lone pair on the water oxygen.
protonated-diazohydroxide.learnerPrompt: Water leaves. Draw how the diazonium ion forms.

mechanismSummary: The amine nitrogen attacks the nitrosonium ion, and loss of a proton gives an N-nitrosamine. Two proton transfers move the hydrogen from nitrogen to oxygen, turning N–N=O into N=N–OH. Protonating that OH makes water a leaving group, and the ring nitrogen's lone pair forms the third N–N bond as water leaves: the aryl diazonium ion, stable only when cold.
